summary: This L0009 run was started by the line's timer, not by an instruction, so there were no 'Asked' items and the answers list is rightly empty. It made no claims and registered no experiments. It wired the plate part of the resting-contact method (Option four) into the event loop on branch method/rest. Every number in evidence/L0009-build-2026-11-25-2.json reproduced in a fresh clone of commit bcd1d5f. The one-sphere check gave one capture, one release, fifteen plate collisions, no energy gains, and energy and momentum residuals no larger than 6.2e-15 and 8.0e-15. The 2D layer stalled in cycle 0 at the same local time, 5.834632169853275. The stall trace matched to the last digit, and its output's SHA-256 matched the recorded one. The method tests gave 45 passed. The frozen engine tests, run with the method off on the branch's engine, gave 74 passed. That settles the point my previous review could not confirm. The line's note and state say what the evidence shows, and the state now says which pieces exist and which do not, as I asked last time. I also checked neighbouring conditions. The stall is not a one-off: with a second seed, and at f* 0.4, the layer also stalls in its first cycle, in the same way. A riding sphere and a sphere sitting diagonally on top of it chatter between capture and pair collision. At Gamma 3, depth 3, three cycles ran without stalling. That supports the state's sentence 'the method cannot run a layer yet' and the reading that moving stacks are the missing piece. One caveat for Chris on the one-sphere books: during a ride, the change in the rider's vertical energy and momentum is booked as plate work and plate impulse by construction (granular/edmd.py, advance_rider). So closing to 1e-14 shows the bookkeeping is consistent, not that the ride is physically right. The independent checks are that the friction loss never turned into a gain and that the capture correction to the height was zero. The ride's vertical motion is exact by definition (the centre sits on the plate), so this hides nothing today. It will matter for stacks, whose heights are integrated. Smaller points. scripts/rest_plate/layer.py crashes on its last print after a cycle-0 stall: it uses a variable that is only set after a completed cycle. The reported result is printed before the crash. The tests again wrote pytest's scratch folders to ~/.tmp (pytest-15 at 09:40 and pytest-16 at 09:46), outside the program's folders. My previous review raised this and it was not acted on. The stack integrator's missed-dip weakness from that review is not fixed yet. It is correctly listed as the first step of 'next', since stacks are not wired in. The question to Chris about whether integrated moving stacks count as time-stepping is still open and honestly framed. program check passes. The latest approval is from 2026-11-24 03:19 UTC, more than a day old.

run_conditions.assessment: The run started at 09:33:18 UTC, eighteen seconds after its scheduled time. It committed its records at 09:49:47 UTC, about sixteen minutes later, well within its limit. It ran on a Linux worker, so the Mac sleep log does not exist and sleep cannot be checked. The work was building code plus short single-threaded checks. Its CPU figure of 0.15 hours is a sum of wall times, as the summary says, and that is plausible: my own reruns of the same checks took a few minutes each. No jobs are in flight (there is no active.jsonl). The scratch folder is empty. The data folder is 683 megabytes of the 15 gigabytes allowed, and 91 gigabytes are free against a floor of 40. The machine did not limit the science. What is left waiting is stage three, moving stacks in the event loop, which the next timer run of this line takes up, and Chris's answer to the time-stepping question.
discrepancies: The summary records the end as 09:52:00Z, but the summary itself was committed at 09:49:47Z. As in the previous run, the end time is a forecast, not a measurement.

The tests wrote pytest's temporary folders to ~/.tmp/pytest-of-roborobo/pytest-15 and pytest-16, outside the two folders the program allows. Passing --basetemp under sequel-data/tmp would fix it. The previous review raised this.
The CPU figure of 0.15 hours comes from wall times, not from ps or logs. The summary says so openly. It is a small departure from CLAUDE.md's 'not an estimate'.
